title: Childhood Communicable Diseases II: Tetanus and Pneumonia
introduction: Tetanus and pneumonia represent two life-threatening infectious emergencies in pediatric and neonatal care. From recognizing lockjaw and preventing spasms in a dark, quiet isolation room to classifying pneumonias, maintaining airway patency, and monitoring respiratory complications, timely medical and nursing interventions are decisive for child survival.
learningOutcomes: 7.1 Explain the aetiology, incubation period, ten points of entry, four clinical classifications, and exotoxin-mediated pathophysiology of tetanus.
7.2 Detail the clinical signs, diagnostic tests (including the Spatula Test), chemotherapy, specialized nursing care, complications, and maternal/infant immunization prevention of tetanus.
7.3 Define pneumonia, classify it by microbiological aetiology, anatomical location, and clinical setting (CAP, HAP, opportunistic, aspiration), and trace its four pathophysiological stages.
7.4 Identify the clinical manifestations, diagnostic investigations, pharmacologic therapy, pneumococcal vaccines, and complications of pneumonia.
7.5 Apply the nursing process to pneumonia care, including oxygen/humidification, directed coughing, therapeutic positioning, chest physiotherapy, hydration, pain control, and prevention.

content.heading: Tetanus: Aetiology, Entry Points, Classification, and Pathophysiology
content.body: Derived from the Greek tetanos ('taut') and teinein ('to stretch'), tetanus is a frequently fatal acute infectious disease characterized by prolonged skeletal muscle spasms (cardiac muscle is spared due to its intrinsic electrical properties). It is caused by Clostridium tetani, a Gram-positive, obligate anaerobic, drumstick-shaped terminal spore-forming rod residing in soil, human, and animal faeces; its spores withstand drying and brief boiling. Incubation ranges from days to months (commonly ~4 days; neonatal tetanus 4–14 days, averaging 7 days)—shorter incubation predicts more severe disease, and untreated neonatal mortality exceeds 90% (80–90% even with treatment). Ten points of entry are: (1) post-traumatic wounds, (2) deep penetrating wounds contaminated with dirt/faeces/saliva, (3) superficial burn wounds, (4) neonatal umbilical cord stump, (5) post-puerperal/post-abortal dirty instruments/dressings, (6) post-surgical bowel pathogens or contaminated instruments, (7) chronic ulcers, guinea worm, or chronic otitis media, (8) cryptogenic/healed invisible wounds, (9) crush injuries, and (10) injuries with devitalized tissue. Clinically, four forms occur: Generalised tetanus (~80% of cases; descending pattern: trismus/lockjaw, risus sardonicus, neck stiffness, dysphagia, pectoral/calf rigidity, opisthotonus, fever, sweating, hypertension/tachycardia, spasms lasting up to 4 weeks); Neonatal tetanus (generalised tetanus from non-sterile umbilical cord cutting in infants of unimmunized mothers, causing ~14% of neonatal deaths in developing nations); Local tetanus (muscle contraction confined near the wound; ~1% fatal, may precede generalised); and Cephalic tetanus (rare, associated with otitis media or head injury affecting facial/cranial nerves, common in children). In anaerobic necrotic wounds, germinating spores release three exotoxins—Tetanospasmin (neurotoxin travelling via peripheral nerves to spinal cord and cranial nerves, causing sensory hypersensitivity and violent motor spasms), non-convulsive neurotoxin, and tetanolysin.

content.heading: Tetanus Clinical Signs, Diagnosis, Chemotherapy, Nursing Management, and Prevention
content.body: Manifestations include irritability, headache, restlessness, low-grade fever, malaise, muscle rigidity, Trismus (lockjaw from spasm of four masticatory muscle sets), Risus Sardonicus (distorted 'social laugh' facial spasm persisting into convalescence), Opisthotonus (severe arched back with retracted head and extended feet risking vertebral fracture), and local spasms. Diagnosis is primarily clinical (distinguishing tetanic spasms from convulsions), supported by the bedside Spatula Test (touching the posterior pharyngeal wall with a sterile soft instrument triggers involuntary jaw clamping if positive, versus a normal gag reflex if negative), arterial blood gases (respiratory status), and specialized toxin demonstration in mice. Medical/chemotherapy principles target four aims: (1) stop toxin production via wound debridement with hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and antibiotics (Metronidazole is the antibiotic of choice; high-dose crystalline penicillin 300 mg / 500,000 IU also eradicates C. tetani); (2) neutralize circulating unbound toxin using Human Tetanus Immunoglobulin (TIG, optionally infiltrated around the wound) or therapeutic Anti-Tetanus Serum (ATS 20,000 IU IM) at separate sites from toxoid; (3) control spasms and autonomic dysfunction with alternating diazepam and chlorpromazine (Largactil), morphine (1 mg/kg), or phenobarbitone (up to 200 mg); and (4) prevent complications via enteral/NG feeding, semi-recumbent positioning, chest physiotherapy, and airway suctioning. Essential nursing gadgets include a padded fracture bed, suction machine, oxygen, tracheotomy tube, drip stand, NG tube, and bed pan. Nurses isolate the child in a dark, quiet room with a 'No-Noise' door notice, handle gently, schedule procedures at peak sedation, maintain a spasm chart (recording spontaneous vs. constant spasms), deliver wound oxygen/H2O2 care, maintain IV/NG hydration and eye/mouth/skin hygiene, monitor for secondary infection, and start physiotherapy on recovery. Complications include malnutrition (from trismus/inability to suck), sepsis, laryngeal spasm/asphyxia, respiratory distress, apnoea/anoxia, pneumonia, atelectasis, vertebral fractures, hypoxic brain damage, and circulatory failure. Prevention combines prompt wound toileting, passive ATS prophylaxis (1,500 IU adults; 750 IU children), sterile hospital delivery/cord cutting, avoiding ear probing, infant DPT immunization (0.5 mL at 6–14 wks), and the 5-dose maternal Tetanus Toxoid (TT 0.5 mL IM) schedule: TT-1 (first contact: 0% protection), TT-2 (≥4 wks: 80%, 3 yrs), TT-3 (≥6 mos: 95%, 5 yrs), TT-4 (≥1 yr: 99%, 10 yrs), and TT-5 (≥1 yr: 99%, lifelong).

content.heading: Pneumonia: Definition, Classifications, Types, Causes, and Pathophysiology
content.body: Pneumonia is an acute microbial inflammation of the lung parenchyma characterized by alveolar oedema and exudate consolidation that impairs gas exchange, affecting 10–20% of children under 5 annually in developing nations (pneumococci are the leading bacterial cause in children). Organisms breach normally sterile lower-airway defences (nasal hairs, mucociliary escalator, epiglottis, cough reflex, IgA, alveolar macrophages) via three routes: aspiration (nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal secretions or oily fluids), inhalation of airborne microbes/pollutants, or hematogenous spread from distant infection. Predisposing factors include bronchial foreign bodies, cold/dampness, pollutants, prior URI, altered consciousness, antibiotic-altered flora, prolonged immobility, airway paralysis, malnutrition, impaired gag/swallow reflex, immunosuppression, intubation, smoking, and aging. Pneumonia is classified by: (A) Microbiological aetiology—viral, bacterial (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Friedlander's/Klebsiella pneumoniae, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Mycoplasma, Legionella, Rickettsia), hypostatic (pooled secretions in bedridden patients), protozoal (Pneumocystis carinii in AIDS/immunocompromised), and fungal; (B) Anatomical location—Bronchopneumonia (diffuse distal airways and alveoli around bronchi, most common in children and elderly), Lobar/Lobular (entire or part of a lobe, more common in adults), and Interstitial (connective tissue); and (C) Primary vs. Secondary (following chemical lung injury or hematogenous spread). Clinically, four major types exist: Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP: onset outside hospital or within first 2 days; ATS Categories 1–4 by outpatient/inpatient/ICU and cardiopulmonary risk); Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP: ≥48 hours post-admission, early <5 days vs. late >5 days, Groups 1–3; Pseudomonas, Enterobacter, S. aureus, S. pneumoniae); Opportunistic Pneumonia (malnutrition, immunodeficiency, transplants, chemo/steroids); and Aspiration Pneumonia (depressed gag/cough reflexes or forceful feeding of babies/children). Pathophysiology progresses through Congestion (capillary permeability leaking serous exudate, fibrinogen, RBCs), Red Hepatization (hyperaemia as microbes multiply), and Gray Hepatization/Consolidation (thick exudates halting gas exchange -> dyspnoea), alongside pleuritic stabbing pain, rusty blood-tinged sputum, dry-to-mucopurulent cough, pyrogen-induced fever, insensible fluid loss, and decreased surfactant causing atelectasis.

content.heading: Pneumonia Manifestations, Investigations, Pharmacotherapy, Vaccines, and Complications
content.body: Key manifestations include dyspnoea, cough (initially dry, later productive with pink/rusty or green/yellow/white purulent sputum—cough in infants <6 weeks strongly suggests pneumonia), stabbing pleuritic chest pain, fever (39.8–40.8°C) with chills and diaphoresis, anorexia, malaise, weak thready pulse, tachypnoea, nasal flaring, shallow grunting respirations, accessory muscle use, percussion dullness over consolidation, increased tactile fremitus, bronchial breath sounds, and crackles/rales/rhonchi/wheezes. Investigations include Chest X-ray (identifies lobar/bronchial distribution, infiltrates, abscess, empyema; may be clear in Mycoplasma), ABGs/pulse oximetry (hypoxaemia/shunting), Gram stain and cultures (sputum collected after mouth rinse via deep cough into sterile container, or suction/bronchoscopy if severe; blood cultures for bacteraemia), CBC (leukocytosis, or leukopenia in AIDS/overwhelming sepsis), elevated ESR, serological titres, and electrolytes (low Na/Cl). Medical management centres on Gram-stain-guided antibiotics initiated within 4 hours of hospital arrival: Penicillin G is the drug of choice for S. pneumoniae (alternatives: erythromycin, clindamycin, 2nd/3rd-gen cephalosporins). Viral pneumonia is managed supportively—antibiotics are used ONLY for secondary bacterial infection. Adjuncts include antipyretics, antitussives, warm moist inhalations, antihistamines, cautious nasal decongestants (excess causes rebound congestion), bed rest, hydration, and oxygen/mechanical ventilation (avoiding high-concentration oxygen in COPD patients to preserve ventilatory drive). Pneumococcal prevention uses Pneumococcal Polysaccharide Vaccine (for high-risk adults/chronic disease) and Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine (PCV13 replacing PCV7, given to infants from 6 weeks). Major complications include shock (may require parenteral corticosteroids), atelectasis, pleural effusion (sterile fluid reabsorbing in 1–2 weeks or aspirated via thoracentesis), pleuritis, lung abscess, and respiratory failure (ARDS).

content.heading: Nursing Management and Prevention of Pneumonia
content.body: Using the nursing process (physical exam, Gordon's typology, CXR), core nursing diagnoses include ineffective airway clearance, activity intolerance, imbalanced nutrition less than body requirements, acute pleuritic pain, and risk for deficient fluid volume, targeting patent airways, energy conservation, normal breathing without hypoxia, adequate nutrition, and zero complications. Key bedside interventions are: (1) Improving Airway Patency & Hydration—encouraging 2–3 L/day fluids (cautiously in heart failure) to thin secretions while keeping strict I&O charts; (2) Oxygen & Humidification—high-humidity face masks delivering warm moist O2/air monitored via pulse oximetry/ABGs; (3) Directed Coughing—positioning, deep inspiration, glottis closure, expiratory contraction against closed glottis, sudden glottis opening, and explosive expiration (plus incentive spirometry and manual lower-rib assistance); (4) Therapeutic Positioning & Chest Physiotherapy—'good lung down' for unilateral disease, right lung down for bilateral disease, semi-Fowler's for rest, and postural drainage/percussion/vibration for >30 mL/day sputum or x-ray mucus plugging/atelectasis, followed by nasotracheal suctioning if cough is weak; (5) Pain, Rest, Nutrition, & Hygiene—analgesics plus relaxation/distraction, clustering care for uninterrupted rest, high-protein/vitamin diet or IV nutrition, and oral/skin care; and (6) Monitoring Complications—expecting antibiotic response within 24–48 hours and investigating persistent/recurrent fever for drug resistance, allergy, superinfection, pleural effusion, or underlying malignancy. Prevention includes discouraging indiscriminate antibiotic use in viral URIs, vaccinating high-risk groups, turning and deep-breathing bedridden/post-op patients, elevating the head during and for ≥30 minutes after NG tube feeds (preferring oral over nasal tubes to prevent nosocomial sinusitis), discouraging force-feeding in children, proper tissue disposal, and prompt URI treatment if symptoms exceed 7 days.

inTextQuestions.question: How is the Spatula Test performed to diagnose tetanus, and what distinguishes a positive result from a negative result?
inTextQuestions.answer: Touch the posterior pharyngeal wall with a sterile, soft-tipped instrument: a positive test triggers involuntary jaw contraction (clamping), whereas a negative test produces a normal gag reflex trying to expel the instrument.

inTextQuestions.question: What are the five doses of the maternal Tetanus Toxoid (TT) schedule and the duration of protection conferred by TT-2 and TT-5?
inTextQuestions.answer: TT-1 (first contact: none), TT-2 (≥4 weeks: 80% for 3 years), TT-3 (≥6 months: 95% for 5 years), TT-4 (≥1 year: 99% for 10 years), and TT-5 (≥1 year: 99% lifelong protection).

inTextQuestions.question: What is the optimal therapeutic lateral positioning for a patient with unilateral versus bilateral pneumonia?
inTextQuestions.answer: For unilateral lung disease, place the unaffected 'good lung down'; for bilateral lung disease, positioning with the right lung down provides the best ventilation and perfusion.

inTextQuestions.question: Within how many hours of hospital arrival should antibiotics be initiated for bacterial pneumonia, and why is high-concentration oxygen contraindicated in COPD patients?
inTextQuestions.answer: Antibiotics should be started promptly within 4 hours of hospital arrival. High-concentration oxygen can depress the hypoxic ventilatory drive in COPD patients, worsening alveolar ventilation and respiratory decompensation.

saqs.question: List the four clinical classifications of tetanus and state any six points of entry for Clostridium tetani.
saqs.answer: Classifications: Generalised tetanus (~80%, descending lockjaw/risus sardonicus/opisthotonus), Neonatal tetanus (non-sterile umbilical cord cutting), Local tetanus (localized spasm near wound), and Cephalic tetanus (cranial/facial nerve involvement from ear/head infection). Six points of entry: post-traumatic wounds, deep penetrating dirty wounds, burns, umbilical cord stump, post-puerperal/abortal contaminated instruments, and crush/dead-tissue injuries (also post-surgical, chronic ulcers/otitis media, healed wounds).

saqs.question: Outline the core chemotherapy principles and eight specialized nursing interventions for managing a child admitted with tetanus.
saqs.answer: Chemotherapy: debride wound with H2O2, administer metronidazole (drug of choice) or high-dose crystalline penicillin to stop toxin production, neutralize unbound toxin with TIG or ATS (20,000 IU IM), and control spasms/ANS instability with alternating diazepam and chlorpromazine (or morphine/phenobarbitone). Nursing care: isolate in a quiet dark room ('No-Noise' sign), admit on padded fracture bed, perform care at peak sedation, handle gently, keep suction/O2/tracheotomy ready, maintain IV/NG fluids and nutrition, open a spasm chart, provide wound H2O2/oxygen care, and initiate physiotherapy during recovery.

saqs.question: Classify pneumonia based on microbiological aetiology and anatomical location, and differentiate Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP) from Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP).
saqs.answer: Microbiological: viral, bacterial (S. pneumoniae, S. aureus, Klebsiella, Mycoplasma, Legionella, Mycobacterium, Rickettsia), hypostatic, protozoal (Pneumocystis carinii), and fungal. Anatomical: bronchopneumonia (diffuse distal airways/alveoli, common in children), lobar/lobular (part/whole lobe, common in adults), and interstitial. CAP begins in the community or within the first 2 days of admission (often S. pneumoniae; ATS Categories 1–4), whereas HAP occurs ≥48 hours after admission in a non-incubating patient (often Pseudomonas, Enterobacter, S. aureus; early <5 days vs. late >5 days).

saqs.question: Trace the pathophysiological stages of pneumonia and list six potential complications.
saqs.answer: Stages: (1) Congestion—dilated capillary permeability leaks serous exudate, fibrinogen, plasma proteins, and RBCs into alveoli; (2) Red Hepatization—hyperaemia and organism proliferation in alveolar fluid; (3) Gray Hepatization/Consolidation—thick exudates fill alveoli making gas exchange impossible (causing dyspnoea), plus reduced surfactant leading to atelectasis. Six complications: shock, atelectasis, pleural effusion, pleuritis, lung abscess, and respiratory failure (ARDS).

saqs.question: Explain the steps of an effective directed cough and outline six nursing measures to prevent pneumonia in hospitalized children and adults.
saqs.answer: Directed cough: assume proper position, perform deep inspiration, close glottis, contract expiratory muscles against closed glottis, suddenly open glottis, and produce explosive expiration. Prevention: avoid indiscriminate antibiotics in minor viral URIs, administer pneumococcal (PCV13/pneumovax) and influenza vaccines, turn unconscious/bedridden patients frequently with deep-breathing/early ambulation, elevate head during and ≥30 min after NG tube feeds (prefer oral tube), discourage force-feeding children, and practise proper cough hygiene/secretion disposal.
